catalog_quote: The Naxi language, spoken in Yunnan, China, has H, M and L tones, plus a marginal Rising tone. This is an ‘easy’ tone system. Tones are lexically attached to syllables and there are extremely few processes of tonal change [20]. Phonetically, the tones are readily identifiable; there are no oppositions in the language that could complicate their production and perception, such as vowel quantity [24], phonation types, distinctive stress, or glottalized consonants [6]. Syllable structure is (C)(G)V+Tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened via its text layers ( layout file lines 81-92 and lines 60-70). Section 1.1 'The tone system of Naxi' on the first page of the paper reads exactly as quoted: 'The Naxi language, spoken in Yunnan, China, has H, M and L tones, plus a marginal Rising tone. This is an 'easy' tone system. Tones are lexically attached to syllables and there are extremely few processes of tonal change [20]. Phonetically, the tones are readily identifiable; there are no oppositions in the language that could complicate their production and perception, such as vowel quantity [24], phonation types, distinctive stress, or glottalized consonants [6]. Syllable structure is (C)(G)V+Tone.' -- verbatim. I also verif…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Naxi is a level-tone language with one lexical tone (H, M, L, marginal rising) per (C)(G)V syllable; the language has no distinctive (lexical) stress. The same author states in French (Michaud 2003, MSLP XIII, postprint p.15-16) that Naxi is a 'langue sans accent lexical' in which every syllable has its own tone, prominence being realised by local intonational means.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress (no word stress posited).
new_statements.exceptions: None at word level. Phrase-level prominence phenomena described elsewhere by Michaud (2005 thesis, 2006 Speech Prosody, 2006 LTBA, 2007 JIPA): emphatic stress (accent d'insistance) and an intonational 'intensive' H tone; intonation-group-final lengthening with F0 lowering; grammatical words prosodically weaker/lower than lexical words and subject to syllable reduction; within a disyllable the second syllable tends to be realised at lower F0 (word-level declination), described as allotonic, not accentual.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the lexical/word level (absence of distinctive stress) for Western (Lijiang-plain) Naxi; recordings made in Lijiang with four native speakers (F2, M5, M7, M9), the same consultants as Michaud's 2005 thesis (main fieldwork village /ɑ̄ ʂə˞̀/, Wenhua, Jinshan township, c. 20 km NE of Lijiang town). Prominence and lengthening effects reported by the author are intonational (phrase/utterance level, carrier-sentence citation forms).
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand statements are by Alexis Michaud on Western Naxi of the Lijiang plain (naxi1245 proper; Glottolog 'Lijiang' dialect area): main fieldwork village /ɑ̄ ʂə˞̀/ (冷不罗, Wenhua 文化 administrative village, Jinshan 金山 township, c. 20 km NE of Lijiang town) plus Lijiang-town speakers; the ICPhS 2015 recordings were made in Lijiang with speakers F2, M5, M7, M9. Not to be confused with Yongning Na / Narua (yong1270) or Laze, sister Naish languages treated in Michaud 2017 and in the ECLL article; the Pianding dialect paper (Michaud & He Likun 2015) describes an eastern-area Naxi variety and is silent on stress.

tone_statements.translation: On monosyllabic words Ciending Naxi shows three tone categories, pronounced Low [11], Mid [33] and high-rising [35]. In the phonemic analysis the high-rising tone can be treated as a simple High tone. These three categories correspond very directly to those of the other dialects of the Lijiang plain (e.g. the Lengbuluo dialect of Wenhua township, surveyed by the author): see Table 1. [...] Table 1 shows that Ciending Naxi has fewer tone categories than the Naxi of Dayan (Lijiang), Lengbuluo etc. The fourth category of the latter dialects (the rising tone) is an innovation; it has some grammatical functions and is very rare in the vocabulary (loanwords apart). In this respect Ciending is more conservative than the four-category dialects of the Lijiang plain. [...] Ciending Naxi has few tone-change (sandhi) phenomena, like the Lijiang-plain dialects such as Dayan and Lengbuluo.

tone_statements.n_tones: 3 (L 11, M 33, H realised 35); no lexical rising category in this variety

sources.note: Exhaustive survey of lexical tones, coalescence sandhi and grammatical tone change shows Naxi 'rising tone' splits into a lexical rising tone (1 subtype, mostly on Chinese loans from old entering-tone words, rare in native vocabulary, hence a late development) and four non-lexical rising contours produced by syllable coalescence and morphotonology, some now lexicalizing; argues the native lexical rising tone arose from such processes rather than directly from loans.
